readerTitle: The coffee chain that sold cups nobody bought
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Luckin Coffee, 2019~2020년 매출 조작) + 가상 사례 (카페 체인 투자, 소스 제조사, B2B 소프트웨어 스타트업)
insight: 매출은 장부에 적힌 숫자가 아니라 독립된 고객의 돈이 실제로 들어오는 흐름이다. 매출을 볼 때는 '누가, 무엇을 받고, 돈을 냈는가'를 따라간다.
misconception: 감사받은 재무제표에 매출이 찍혀 있고 빠르게 늘고 있으면 그 매출은 진짜다.

sources.text: Luckin Coffee, press release on internal investigation (April 2, 2020)
U.S. SEC, press release on settled charges against Luckin Coffee (December 2020)
Muddy Waters Research, publication of an anonymous short-seller report on Luckin Coffee (January 31, 2020)
카페 체인, 소스 제조사, 소프트웨어 스타트업 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Luckin 설립(2017년)과 나스닥 상장(2019년 5월) 시점을 다시 확인하세요.
2020년 4월 2일 발표의 조작 매출 규모(2019년 2~4분기, 약 22억 위안)를 회사 발표문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 "about 2.2 billion yuan"으로 적었습니다.
SEC 합의 금액 $180 million(2020년 12월)과 나스닥 상장폐지(2020년 여름) 시점을 확인하세요.
Muddy Waters가 공개한 익명 보고서가 매장 영상 수천 시간 분석에 근거했다는 점을 확인하세요. 구체적 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
조작이 회계감사 과정에서 드러났다는 서술은 여러 보도에 근거합니다. 카드에는 일반적으로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 확인하세요.
가상 소프트웨어 사례 계산: 계약 $400,000, 같은 고객에게 지급하는 '공동 마케팅' 비용 $380,000 → 실제 순유입 $20,000.

cards.title: The coffee chain that sold cups nobody bought
body: Luckin Coffee opened its first stores in China in 2017. Within about two years it had thousands of locations and a listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange.
Its sales were growing faster than almost anyone's. Then, in April 2020, the company admitted that a large share of those sales had never happened.

image.label: Rows of coffee cups, most of them transparent outlines
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 카운터 위에 커피 컵이 길게 줄지어 있는데 앞쪽 몇 개만 진짜 컵이고 나머지는 점선 윤곽만 있는 유령 컵. 실제 브랜드 로고나 컵 디자인은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A café chain wants your money.
body: A regional café chain asks you to invest. Its sales grew 60% last year, far faster than rivals. The statements are neat and professionally prepared.
You have time for one deep check. Which tells you most about whether the sales are real?

options.text: Read the prepared statements closely, line by line
options.feedback: You'll learn how the business describes itself. But if sales were invented, the statements will be consistent with the invention.

options.text: Compare the growth rate with the rest of the industry
options.feedback: Unusual growth is a reason to look harder, not proof of anything. Real winners also outgrow their rivals.

options.text: Match reported sales to money arriving from card processors and real store traffic
options.feedback: It's slower and messier, but it checks the one thing fake sales can't easily copy: cash from outside customers who actually showed up.

cards.title: Thousands of hours of store video.
body: In January 2020, a short-seller firm published an anonymous report built on thousands of hours of video from Luckin stores. Its claim: far fewer orders were coming through the doors than the company reported.
Luckin denied it. Weeks later, it announced that an internal investigation had found the chief operating officer and staff had fabricated about **2.2 billion yuan** in 2019 sales.
The shares were delisted from the Nasdaq that year. Luckin later paid $180 million to settle U.S. securities charges.

cards.title: Revenue that isn't real
body: **Revenue that isn't real** is a sale on the books with no independent customer paying real money for something they actually received.
Invention, like at Luckin, is the extreme case. More common versions are quieter: a company and a partner buying from each other in a circle, or stock pushed onto distributors who can send it back.
All share one test. Follow the money. If it doesn't arrive from an outside customer, the sale is a story, not revenue.

image.label: Two arrows: one from a customer, one looping back to the seller
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 '고객 → 돈 → 가게' 한 방향 화살표(진짜 매출, 초록). 오른쪽은 가게에서 나간 돈이 파트너를 거쳐 다시 가게로 돌아오는 원형 화살표(가짜 매출, 빨강). 라벨은 영어 "Real sale", "Round trip".

cards.title: Four questions to ask about any sales number.
body: Fake or inflated sales usually leave marks somewhere outside the sales line.
list: **Where's the cash?** Sales rise, but bank deposits don't rise with them
**Who's the customer?** Big buyers linked to owners, staff or the company itself
**When did it happen?** Unusual spikes in the last days of a quarter or year
**Is money flowing both ways?** The customer also gets paid by the seller
cards.callout: One mark is a question. Several together are a red flag.

cards.title: A full warehouse isn't a sale.
body: A sauce maker is short of its yearly target. In late December, it ships distributors three months of extra stock, with the right to return anything unsold.
The year's sales look great. In spring, the returns arrive and January orders dry up, because distributors are still full.
Nothing was invented here. But the customers didn't really want those jars yet. Pulling future sales forward makes this year look better and next year look worse.

image.label: A distributor's warehouse overflowing with sauce jars
image.brief: 창고 선반이 소스 병으로 넘쳐 바닥까지 쌓인 장면. 달력은 12월 31일. 한쪽에 "Returns"라고 적힌 상자들이 대기 중. 실제 브랜드 라벨은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Not every gap means fake.
body: Cash and sales often disagree for honest reasons. A caterer may invoice a wedding today and get paid in 30 days. A software firm may bill a year upfront.
Real customers who simply pay late are a different problem, covered in the next lesson.
So treat the four questions as a reason to dig, not as a verdict. And remember that people who fake sales also prepare answers. Check the evidence, not just the explanation.

cards.title: Now it's a software startup.
body: You're about to invest in a B2B software startup. Its biggest new deal is a $400,000 yearly contract, signed on the last day of the quarter.
In the same week, the startup agreed to pay that customer $380,000 for "joint marketing." What do you do?

options.text: Count it at $400,000. Marketing is a separate cost
options.feedback: On paper they're two deals. In cash terms, the startup is mostly paying for its own sale, and only $20,000 really comes in from outside.

options.text: Ask for both contracts and treat the deal as about $20,000 until the marketing is shown to be real
options.feedback: You may undervalue a genuine partnership for a while. But you're judging the business on money that truly arrives, not a circle.

options.text: Walk away from the investment immediately
options.feedback: You avoid the risk, but you may be dropping a good company over one deal you never examined. A few questions cost less.

cards.title: Revenue is money from a real customer, not a number on a page.
body: Before trusting a sales figure, ask who paid, for what, and where the cash went.
**Try it today:** take last month's sales for your own business. Compare them with deposits from customers. Can you explain the gap in one sentence?
